chunks: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Abu Abdillah, from Muhammad ibn Abdillah ibn Mihran, from Ali ibn Ja'far, from his brother Musa ibn Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said:

I asked him about a man who dedicates to the Ka'bah such and such, what is upon him if he is unable to provide what he dedicated? He (AS) said: If he made it a vow and does not own it, there is nothing upon him. And if it is from what he owns, such as a slave boy or girl or similar, he sells it and buys perfume with its price and perfumes the Ka'bah with it. And if it is an animal, there is nothing upon him.

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: The discussion regarding these narrations is like the discussion regarding the narrations we presented earlier concerning the expiation of an oath. And that depends on the state of the man. Thus it is in the expiation of the vow, because whoever is able to free a slave, or feed sixty poor people, or fast two consecutive months, does whichever he wishes. And when he is unable to do that, the expiation of the oath is upon him. If he is unable to do that as well, then forgiveness is upon him and there is nothing else.

key_terms.نَذْرٌ: Vow or dedication of a specific item or act to God or a sacred place

ai.seo_question: What is the expiation for a person who vows to dedicate an item to the Ka'bah but cannot fulfill the vow?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi records this ruling from Imam al-Sadiq (AS), clarifying that if the vowed item is owned but not immediately available, the vowholder must sell it to purchase perfume for the Ka'bah, whereas if it is an animal, no compensation is due. The text explicitly links the expiation for breaking a vow to the hierarchy of expiating an oath (kaffarat al-yamin), establishing a graduated scale of obligation based on the individual's financial capacity, from freeing a slave to fasting and finally mere istighfar.
